coverage: Named roster: FETCHED AT PRIMARY - Peterson (the Game Wizards excerpt at Polygon plus two further Playing at the World posts; the predecessor had Quagmire! and the blog), Zagal and Deterding (chapter 1 accepted manuscript at White Rose eprints), Appelcline (Designers & Dragons column #24 via a Wayback raw capture, live rpg.net 403s), Merwin's sibling columns 624 and 626, and the 4e delve-format thread through Cordell's own words quoted at length on Greyhawkery, Slavicsek's introduction quoted on The Alexandrian, Decker and Noonan's 2005 Wizards column recovered from the Wayback Machine, Delta's Gygax-only encounter-text series, and the Welcome to the Deathtrap layout history; Holmes/Moldvay/Mentzer Basic as register history through Zach Howard's manuscript-versus-published series (Howard is the co-author of the blocked chapter 5) and two later essays. BLOCKED - Fifty Years of D&D chapters 3, 5, 15 and 17 (DOIs, authors and page ranges resolved through Crossref, but direct.mit.edu returns 403 to curl and to WebFetch, no Wayback capture exists, and neither OpenAlex nor Semantic Scholar holds an abstract; reached only at one remove through Stuart Gorman's review); Fine's Shared Fantasy and Mackay's Fantasy Role-Playing Game (archive.org search-inside endpoints return HTTP 000 from this host); Baur's 'How to Design a City State, Tribe, or Nation' (anyflip serves the flipbook shell only, pdfcoffee is behind Cloudflare, Google Books was quota-blocked all day; reached at one remove through a Gnome Stew review that quotes it with a page cite and through Baur's own 2025 seminar transcript). NOT FOUND at any open route - Witwer and Riggs; Garcia 2017 is confirmed CLOSED with its abstract elided, and Shank 2015 remains abstract-only (both already logged by the predecessor). Substantive sources this run: 27 - 20 by direct fetch, 2 by Wayback raw capture, 3 by PDF binary plus pypdf extraction, 2 reached only through a quoting source. Every one of the 112 quotations was re-checked as an exact substring of the page as fetched. A finding in its own right: the register of published D&D place description is essentially unstudied - Carbonell says in his own words that role-playing gametexts are "an overlooked area of investigation for literary scholars", Deterding and Zagal's field survey files textual work under one chapter, and the sharpest measurements of how a settlement is described come not from scholarship but from designers (Cook, Baur, Decker and Noonan) and from OSR bloggers counting words.
